'''Kenneth R. Poeppelmeier''' (born 1949) is an American [[Solid-state chemistry|solid-state chemist]] who holds the Charles E. and Emma H. Morrison Professorship of Chemistry at [[Northwestern University]].<ref name="NU">{{cite web |title=Kenneth R. Poeppelmeier |url=https://chemistry.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/profiles/kenneth-poeppelmeier.html |website=Department of Chemistry |publisher=Northwestern University |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref> After a doctorate at [[Iowa State University]], he spent six years in industrial research at Exxon Research and Engineering Company, and he moved to Northwestern in 1984.<ref name="CIC2bio">{{cite web |title=Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry II, 2nd Edition: Editors |url=https://shop.elsevier.com/books/comprehensive-inorganic-chemistry-ii/reedijk/978-0-08-097774-4 |publisher=Elsevier |access-date=October 13, 2026}}</ref> Between 2010 and 2020 he also held a joint appointment at [[Argonne National Laboratory]].<ref name="CV">{{cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae – Kenneth R. Poeppelmeier |url=https://www.flogen.org/sips2023/pdfs/Kenneth_Poeppelmeier_Cv.pdf |publisher=FLOGEN Stars Outreach (Sustainable Industrial Processing Summit 2023) |format=PDF |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref>

His research deals with how inorganic solids, chiefly mixed metal oxides and compounds with more than one kind of anion, can be made, how their atoms are arranged, and what properties follow.<ref name="Anales2017">{{cite journal |title=Kenneth R. Poeppelmeier, Socio de Honor de la RSEQ |department=Noticias |journal=Anales de Química |volume=113 |issue=3 |page=203 |year=2017 |publisher=Real Sociedad Española de Química |url=https://analesdequimica.es/index.php/AnalesQuimica/article/download/1038/1399 |language=es}}</ref> Topics have included crystals that lack a center of symmetry and are used in [[nonlinear optics]], cation ordering in [[Perovskite (structure)|perovskite]] oxides, [[Transparent conducting film|transparent conducting oxides]], and solids for catalysis and batteries.<ref name="Li2019">{{cite journal |last=Li |first=Yadong |title=A solid-state chemist's eye for the development of materials science in China |journal=Science China Materials |volume=62 |issue=12 |pages=1783–1787 |date=2019 |doi=10.1007/s40843-019-1194-0}}</ref> A 1998 review of noncentrosymmetric oxides that he wrote with P. Shiv Halasyamani was later featured by ''[[Chemistry of Materials]]'' among its papers cited more than 1,000 times.<ref name="CM1k">{{cite journal |last1=Goring |first1=Paul |last2=Skrabalak |first2=Sara E. |title=Foreseeing the Future of Noncentrosymmetric Oxides: An Interview with Kenneth Poeppelmeier for Chemistry of Materials' 1k Club |journal=Chemistry of Materials |volume=36 |issue=9 |pages=3979–3980 |date=May 14, 2024 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c01187}}</ref> In 2016 his group and co-workers reported optical activity in a crystal grown from a [[racemic mixture]], and in 2025 a collaboration that included his group reported a centrosymmetric crystal that absorbs left- and right-handed [[circular polarization|circularly polarized]] light unequally.<ref name="Gautier2016">{{cite journal |last1=Gautier |first1=Romain |last2=Klingsporn |first2=Jordan M. |last3=Van Duyne |first3=Richard P. |last4=Poeppelmeier |first4=Kenneth R. |title=Optical activity from racemates |journal=Nature Materials |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=591–592 |date=2016 |doi=10.1038/nmat4628}}</ref><ref name="CEN2025">{{cite news |last=Peplow |first=Mark |title=Crystals defy their symmetry to discern chiral light |url=https://cen.acs.org/physical-chemistry/Crystals-defy-symmetry-discern-chiral/103/web/2025/06 |work=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] |date=June 23, 2025 |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref>

Poeppelmeier was an associate editor of ''[[Inorganic Chemistry (journal)|Inorganic Chemistry]]'' from 1993 to 2013, and with Jan Reedijk he edited the multi-volume reference works ''Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry II'' (2013) and ''Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry III'' (2023).<ref name="CV" /><ref name="CIC2">{{cite book |editor1-last=Reedijk |editor1-first=Jan |editor2-last=Poeppelmeier |editor2-first=Kenneth |title=Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry II: From Elements to Applications |edition=2nd |publisher=Elsevier |year=2013 |isbn=978-0-08-096529-1}}</ref><ref name="CIC3">{{cite book |editor1-last=Reedijk |editor1-first=Jan |editor2-last=Poeppelmeier |editor2-first=Kenneth R. |title=Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry III |edition=3rd |publisher=Elsevier |year=2023 |isbn=978-0-12-823144-9 |url=https://shop.elsevier.com/books/comprehensive-inorganic-chemistry-iii/reedijk/978-0-12-823144-9}}</ref> He became a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1993, and in 2016 Spain's [[Royal Academy of Exact, Physical and Natural Sciences]] named him a foreign corresponding member.<ref name="NU" /><ref name="RAC">{{cite web |title=Profesor Kenneth R. Poeppelmeier |url=https://rac.es/sobre-nosotros/miembros/academicos/correspondiente-internacional/981/ |publisher=Real Academia de Ciencias Exactas, Físicas y Naturales |language=es |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref> Other recognition includes honorary membership of the [[Spanish Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 2017, the Tianshan Award for 2020 from the [[Xinjiang]] regional government, and the Fray International Sustainability Award from FLOGEN Stars Outreach in 2023.<ref name="Anales2017" /><ref name="Tianshan">{{cite news |last=Kang |first=Haoyan |script-title=zh:5名专家获2020年度自治区外国专家“天山奖” |trans-title=Five experts receive the autonomous region's 2020 Tianshan Award for foreign experts |url=http://news.ts.cn/system/2021/05/11/036629013.shtml |work=Tianshan Net – [[Xinjiang Daily]] |date=May 11, 2021 |language=zh |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref><ref name="FLOGEN2023">{{cite web |title=Fray International Sustainability Award |url=https://www.flogen.org/?p=38 |publisher=FLOGEN Stars Outreach |access-date=October 13, 2026}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Poeppelmeier was born in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1949.<ref name="RAC" /> He studied chemistry at the [[University of Missouri]] in Columbia and graduated with a B.S. in 1971.<ref name="CIC2bio" /> For the next three years he was a [[Peace Corps]] volunteer, teaching chemistry at [[Samoa College]] in [[Samoa|Western Samoa]].<ref name="CIC2bio" /> He then entered graduate school at Iowa State University, joined the group of [[John Corbett (chemist)|John D. Corbett]], and completed his Ph.D. in 1978.<ref name="CIC2bio" /> His doctoral papers with Corbett described reduced [[scandium]] chlorides containing metal–metal bonds, including the chain compound Sc<sub>5</sub>Cl<sub>8</sub>.<ref name="Poeppelmeier1978">{{cite journal |last1=Poeppelmeier |first1=Kenneth R. |last2=Corbett |first2=John D. |title=Cluster condensation reactions. Synthesis and structure of pentascandium octachloride (Sc5Cl8). An infinite chain structure derived by cluster condensation |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=100 |issue=16 |pages=5039–5044 |date=1978 |doi=10.1021/ja00484a021}}</ref> In a later study published in 1985, Poeppelmeier, Shiou-Jyh Hwu and Corbett examined interstitial carbon atoms in a related compound, Sc<sub>7</sub>Cl<sub>10</sub>C<sub>2</sub>.<ref name="Hwu1985">{{cite journal |last1=Hwu |first1=Shiou-Jyh |last2=Corbett |first2=John D. |last3=Poeppelmeier |first3=Kenneth R. |title=Interstitial atoms in metal-metal bonded arrays: The synthesis and characterization of heptascandium decachlorodicarbide, Sc7Cl10C2, and comparison with the interstitial-free Sc7Cl10 |journal=Journal of Solid State Chemistry |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=43–58 |date=1985 |doi=10.1016/S0022-4596(85)80059-1}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1978 Poeppelmeier joined the corporate research laboratories of Exxon Research and Engineering Company and advanced from research chemist to senior staff chemist.<ref name="CV" /> Working with John Longo and Allan Jacobson, he prepared mixed metal oxides, determined their structures and tested them as [[Heterogeneous catalysis|heterogeneous catalysts]].<ref name="CIC2bio" /> Papers from this period described calcium manganese oxides, CaMnO<sub>2.5</sub> and Ca<sub>2</sub>MnO<sub>3.5</sub>, whose structures are perovskites with ordered oxygen vacancies.<ref name="Poeppelmeier1982">{{cite journal |last1=Poeppelmeier |first1=K. R. |last2=Leonowicz |first2=M. E. |last3=Longo |first3=J. M. |title=CaMnO2.5 and Ca2MnO3.5: New oxygen-defect perovskite-type oxides |journal=Journal of Solid State Chemistry |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=89–98 |date=1982 |doi=10.1016/0022-4596(82)90404-2}}</ref>

He joined Northwestern's chemistry department in 1984 as an associate professor, became a full professor in 1988 and was appointed to the Morrison chair in 2010.<ref name="CV" /><ref name="NU" /> From 1989 to 2000 he was associate director of the Science and Technology Center for Superconductivity, a [[National Science Foundation]] center shared by Northwestern, the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], the [[University of Chicago]] and Argonne.<ref name="CV" /><ref name="NSF">{{cite web |title=Award 9120000: Science and Technology Center for Superconductivity |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/show-award?AWD_ID=9120000 |publisher=National Science Foundation |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref> He was associate division director for science in Argonne's Chemical Sciences and Engineering Division from 2010 to 2020. From 2012 to 2020, he directed Northwestern's Center for Catalysis and Surface Science.<ref name="CV" /> Earlier, in 1988–89, he chaired the Solid State Subdivision of the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Division of Inorganic Chemistry.<ref name="CV" />

==Research==
In a 2019 editorial in ''Science China Materials'', Tsinghua University professor Yadong Li surveyed Poeppelmeier's work. Its references cover noncentrosymmetric crystals, oxygen-deficient and cation-ordered perovskites, oxide surfaces, transparent conducting oxides, phosphors and racemic crystals.<ref name="Li2019" /> The Spanish chemical society's journal, reporting his honorary membership, pointed to the breadth of the compounds his group had made, from halides, sulfides, antimonides and phosphates to oxyfluorides and many perovskite-type oxides, and to the electrical, magnetic, catalytic, optical and electrochemical behavior examined in them.<ref name="Anales2017" />

===Noncentrosymmetric and optical materials===
Only crystals without a center of inversion can show effects such as [[piezoelectricity]], [[pyroelectricity]] and [[second-harmonic generation]], so finding such structures is a goal in the search for optical materials.<ref name="Halasyamani1998">{{cite journal |last1=Halasyamani |first1=P. Shiv |last2=Poeppelmeier |first2=Kenneth R. |title=Noncentrosymmetric Oxides |journal=Chemistry of Materials |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=2753–2769 |date=1998 |doi=10.1021/cm980140w}}</ref> In their 1998 review, Poeppelmeier and Halasyamani, who was then his graduate student, sorted close to 600 noncentrosymmetric oxides listed in the 1996 Inorganic Crystal Structure Database by crystal class and by the coordination of their metal ions.<ref name="CM1k" /> The review appeared in a ''Chemistry of Materials'' special issue that Poeppelmeier guest-edited.<ref name="Preface1998">{{cite journal |last=Poeppelmeier |first=Kenneth R. |title=Preface to the Special Issue: Frontiers in Inorganic Solid-State Chemistry |journal=Chemistry of Materials |volume=10 |issue=10 |pages=2577–2578 |date=1998 |doi=10.1021/cm981002+}}</ref> Writing in 2024, the journal's editors highlighted its observation that roughly four in five of these oxides contain a cation prone to a second-order [[Jahn–Teller effect|Jahn–Teller]] distortion or one in tetrahedral coordination, a pattern that suggested where to look for new examples.<ref name="CM1k" /> With collaborators he later co-wrote reviews of crystals for nonlinear optics in the deep ultraviolet and of borates as optical materials.<ref name="Tran2016">{{cite journal |last1=Tran |first1=T. Thao |last2=Yu |first2=Hongwei |last3=Rondinelli |first3=James M. |last4=Poeppelmeier |first4=Kenneth R. |last5=Halasyamani |first5=P. Shiv |title=Deep Ultraviolet Nonlinear Optical Materials |journal=Chemistry of Materials |volume=28 |issue=15 |pages=5238–5258 |date=2016 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemmater.6b02366}}</ref><ref name="Mutailipu2021">{{cite journal |last1=Mutailipu |first1=Miriding |last2=Poeppelmeier |first2=Kenneth R. |last3=Pan |first3=Shilie |title=Borates: A Rich Source for Optical Materials |journal=Chemical Reviews |volume=121 |issue=3 |pages=1130–1202 |date=2021 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemrev.0c00796}}</ref>

===Perovskites, oxide surfaces and transparent conductors===
A 1993 review from his group examined how two different cations are arranged on the B site of double perovskite oxides.<ref name="Anderson1993">{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Mark T. |last2=Greenwood |first2=Kevin B. |last3=Taylor |first3=Gregg A. |last4=Poeppelmeier |first4=Kenneth R. |title=B-cation arrangements in double perovskites |journal=Progress in Solid State Chemistry |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=197–233 |date=1993 |doi=10.1016/0079-6786(93)90004-B}}</ref> With [[Laurence D. Marks]] and others he reported the atomic structure of a titanium-rich [[strontium titanate]] surface in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' in 2002.<ref name="Erdman2002">{{cite journal |last1=Erdman |first1=Natasha |last2=Poeppelmeier |first2=Kenneth R. |last3=Asta |first3=Mark |last4=Warschkow |first4=Oliver |last5=Ellis |first5=Donald E. |last6=Marks |first6=Laurence D. |title=The structure and chemistry of the TiO2-rich surface of SrTiO3 (001) |journal=Nature |volume=419 |issue=6902 |pages=55–58 |date=2002 |doi=10.1038/nature01010}}</ref> Northwestern collaborations with Thomas Mason, [[Tobin J. Marks]] and Arthur Freeman explored chemical and thin-film routes to new transparent conducting oxides,<ref name="Freeman2000">{{cite journal |last1=Freeman |first1=A. J. |last2=Poeppelmeier |first2=K. R. |last3=Mason |first3=T. O. |last4=Chang |first4=R. P. H. |last5=Marks |first5=T. J. |title=Chemical and Thin-Film Strategies for New Transparent Conducting Oxides |journal=MRS Bulletin |volume=25 |issue=8 |pages=45–51 |date=2000 |doi=10.1557/mrs2000.150}}</ref> and his group described hydrothermal methods for making [[delafossite]]-type oxides.<ref name="Sheets2006">{{cite journal |last1=Sheets |first1=William C. |last2=Mugnier |first2=Elodie |last3=Barnabé |first3=Antoine |last4=Marks |first4=Tobin J. |last5=Poeppelmeier |first5=Kenneth R. |title=Hydrothermal Synthesis of Delafossite-Type Oxides |journal=Chemistry of Materials |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=7–20 |date=2006 |doi=10.1021/cm051791c}}</ref> His lecture at the 2017 Madrid session in his honor dealt with [[indium tin oxide]] and other conducting oxides in which other elements replace part of the indium or tin.<ref name="UCM">{{cite web |last=Fernández |first=Jaime |title=Químicas homenajea al profesor Kenneth Poeppelmeier |url=http://webs.ucm.es/BUCM/revcul/tribunacomplutense/197/art2767.php |website=Tribuna Complutense |publisher=Universidad Complutense de Madrid |date=May 11, 2017 |language=es |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref>

===Mixed-anion compounds, catalysis and energy storage===
Poeppelmeier has also worked on solids that pair oxide with fluoride or other anions. Along with six other authors, including professor Hiroshi Kageyama, he co-authored a 2018 review in ''[[Nature Communications]]'' that presented multiple-anion compounds as an expanding area of materials chemistry and physics.<ref name="Kageyama2018">{{cite journal |last1=Kageyama |first1=Hiroshi |last2=Hayashi |first2=Katsuro |last3=Maeda |first3=Kazuhiko |last4=Attfield |first4=J. Paul |last5=Hiroi |first5=Zenji |last6=Rondinelli |first6=James M. |last7=Poeppelmeier |first7=Kenneth R. |title=Expanding frontiers in materials chemistry and physics with multiple anions |journal=Nature Communications |volume=9 |article-number=772 |date=2018 |doi=10.1038/s41467-018-02838-4  |doi-access=free|pmc=5823932 |pmid=29472526}}</ref> A 2016 collaborative study reported that magnesium ions could be inserted into and removed from a layered oxyfluoride, which was examined as a cathode for magnesium batteries.<ref name="Incorvati2016">{{cite journal |last1=Incorvati |first1=Jared T. |last2=Wan |first2=Liwen F. |last3=Key |first3=Baris |last4=Zhou |first4=Dehua |last5=Liao |first5=Chen |last6=Fuoco |first6=Lindsay |last7=Holland |first7=Michael |last8=Wang |first8=Hao |last9=Prendergast |first9=David |last10=Poeppelmeier |first10=Kenneth R. |last11=Vaughey |first11=John T. |title=Reversible Magnesium Intercalation into a Layered Oxyfluoride Cathode |journal=Chemistry of Materials |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=17–20 |date=2016 |doi=10.1021/acs.chemmater.5b02746}}</ref> Poeppelmeier's research on oxide catalysis began during his time at Exxon and continued at Northwestern. From 2012 to 2020, he also directed Northwestern's Center for Catalysis and Surface Science.<ref name="CIC2bio" /><ref name="CV" />

===Chirality and polarized light===
In 2016 Poeppelmeier, Romain Gautier of the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research|CNRS]] and colleagues reported in ''[[Nature Materials]]'' that a solid made from equal amounts of two mirror-image forms can be optically active when the molecules pack in certain crystal classes.<ref name="Gautier2016" /> According to Northwestern's account, the team designed the material in one of the four arrangements expected to allow [[circular dichroism]], and Richard Van Duyne's group measured its response.<ref name="NU2016">{{cite news |last=Fellman |first=Megan |title=One minus one does not always equal zero in chemistry |url=https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2016/04/one-minus-one-does-not-always-equal-zero-in-chemistry |work=Northwestern Now |publisher=Northwestern University |date=April 26, 2016 |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref> A 2023 paper by his group used the symmetry groupings of the 1998 review to analyze how racemic crystals lose inversion symmetry.<ref name="Wang2023">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yiran |last2=Nisbet |first2=Matthew L. |last3=Kamp |first3=Kendall R. |last4=Hiralal |first4=Emily |last5=Gautier |first5=Romain |last6=Halasyamani |first6=P. Shiv |last7=Poeppelmeier |first7=Kenneth R. |title=Beyond π–π Stacking: Understanding Inversion Symmetry Breaking in Crystalline Racemates |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=145 |issue=30 |pages=16879–16888 |date=2023 |doi=10.1021/jacs.3c05380}}</ref><ref name="CM1k" />

In 2025 a Northwestern–[[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] team reported in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' that the centrosymmetric crystal Li<sub>2</sub>Co<sub>3</sub>(SeO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub> absorbs left- and right-circularly polarized light to different extents.<ref name="Parrish2025">{{cite journal |last1=Parrish |first1=Katherine A. |last2=Salij |first2=Andrew |last3=Kamp |first3=Kendall R. |display-authors=etal |title=Differential absorption of circularly polarized light by a centrosymmetric crystal |journal=Science |volume=388 |issue=6752 |pages=1194–1197 |date=June 12, 2025 |doi=10.1126/science.adr5478 |pmid=40504909}} Correction: {{cite journal |title=Erratum for the Research Article 'Differential absorption of circularly polarized light by a centrosymmetric crystal' by K. A. Parrish et al. |journal=Science |volume=389 |issue=6766 |article-number=eaec1372 |date=September 18, 2025 |doi=10.1126/science.aec1372}}</ref> The theory was led by Roel Tempelaar, the work was co-led by Poeppelmeier and Randall Goldsmith, and Poeppelmeier's group synthesized the crystals.<ref name="NUcpl2025">{{cite web |title=Symmetrical crystals can absorb light asymmetrically |url=https://chemistry.northwestern.edu/about/news/2025/symetrically-shaped-crystals-can-absorb-light-asymetrically.html |website=Department of Chemistry |publisher=Northwestern University |year=2025 |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref> The authors traced the effect to interference between [[linear dichroism]] and linear [[birefringence]], and the signal reversed when the sample was flipped.<ref name="Parrish2025" /> Reports in ''Chemical & Engineering News'' and ''[[Chemistry World]]'' presented the result as running against the long-standing expectation that centrosymmetric crystals cannot show such chiroptical behavior.<ref name="CEN2025" /><ref name="ChemWorld2025">{{cite news |last=Demming |first=Anna |title=Centrosymmetric crystal displays chiral optical responses previously believed to be impossible |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/centrosymmetric-crystal-displays-chiral-optical-responses-previously-believed-to-be-impossible/4021770.article |work=Chemistry World |date=June 30, 2025 |access-date=October 9, 2026}}</ref>

==Editorial work and honors==
Poeppelmeier sat on the editorial board of ''Chemistry of Materials'' from 1990 to 1995 and served as an associate editor of ''Inorganic Chemistry'' for two decades, from 1993 to 2013; Northwestern lists a 2013 recognition for twenty years of service to that journal.<ref name="CV" /><ref name="NU" /><ref name="Anales2017" /> He has served on the editorial boards of several journals, including ''Journal of Alloys and Compounds'' and ''Solid State Sciences'', and more recently ''Science China Materials'', whose board he joined in 2014.<ref name="CIC2bio" /><ref name="CV" /> He and Jan Reedijk were the editors of the nine-volume second edition of ''Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry'' (2013), which was planned as a successor to the 1973 original, and of the ten-volume third edition (2023).<ref name="CIC2bio" /><ref name="CIC2" /><ref name="CIC3" />

He was elected a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1993. Northwestern's list of his honors also includes a fellowship of the [[Japan Society for the Promotion of Science]] in 1997 and a professorship of the [[Institut Universitaire de France]] in 2003.<ref name="NU" /> He received two National Science Foundation Creativity Extension Awards, in 2000 and 2022.<ref name="CIC2bio" />

The Royal Academy of Exact, Physical and Natural Sciences named him a foreign corresponding member on June 22, 2016.<ref name="RAC" /> In February 2017 the governing board of the Spanish Royal Society of Chemistry made him an honorary member. He received the appointment in May 2017 at the Faculty of Chemistry of the [[Complutense University of Madrid]], during a scientific session held in his honor by the society's solid-state chemistry group.<ref name="Anales2017" /> He had been a visiting professor at the Complutense in 2009.<ref name="UCM" />

Northwestern lists several Chinese lectureships, beginning with one from the National Natural Science Foundation of China in 1999, and a visiting professorship at the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in 2011.<ref name="NU" /> In May 2021 the ''Xinjiang Daily'' reported that he was one of five recipients of the 2020 Tianshan Award, the highest honor the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region gives to foreign experts; the newspaper named him as an expert engaged by the academy's Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry.<ref name="Tianshan" />

In 2023 Poeppelmeier received the Fray International Sustainability Award from FLOGEN Stars Outreach at the Sustainable Industrial Processing Summit in Panama, for his work in solid-state materials chemistry.<ref name="FLOGEN2023" />
